\chapter{Reading — Objects, Places, and a Day}
\label{ch:la-dies-meus}
\hlchaptermodality{59}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can track direct objects and place phrases through a social exchange and a short first-person account without translating sentence by sentence.}

A 140-word adapted account whose time anchors, place phrases and visible object endings let a beginning reader follow one full day.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[aqua -> aquam; epistula -> epistulam …]{aqua -> aquam — when the action reaches the thing}

\label{lesson:LA-C59-a-objects}



\begin{quote}
You already know \textbf{aqua}: water. Read one new sentence.

\textbf{Aquam bibō.} — I drink water.

Nothing new has happened to the water. Its ending changed because it is now the thing the action reaches.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: -a becomes -am}
Latin marks the direct object with the accusative case. For the familiar nouns ending in \textbf{-a}, the first useful move is small:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{aqua -> aquam} — I drink \textbf{aquam}
  \item \textbf{epistula -> epistulam} — I write \textbf{epistulam}
  \item \textbf{porta -> portam} — I open \textbf{portam}
\end{itemize}

The \textbf{-m} is a reading signal. It tells you that this word receives the action even if Latin moves the word somewhere English would not.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: actor, action, object}]
In \textbf{epistulam scrībō}, the verb \textbf{scrībō} already says \textquotedblleft{}I write.\textquotedblright{} The ending \textbf{-am} tells you what I write.

Read from the endings rather than from position: \textbf{portam aperiō} and \textbf{aperiō portam} mean the same basic thing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item aquam bibō — the water receives the action
  \item epistulam scrībō — the letter receives the action
  \item portam aperiō — the gate receives the action
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{-am} tell you here? (\textbf{This familiar -a noun is the direct object.})

Change \textbf{epistula} for \textquotedblleft{}I write a letter.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Epistulam scrībō.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[amicus -> amicum; magister -> …]{amīcus -> amīcum — a second road to the same object marker}

\label{lesson:LA-C59-m-objects}



\begin{quote}
You saw \textbf{-a -> -am}. Now read \textbf{amīcum videō} — I see the friend.

The noun changed more visibly, but the final signal is familiar: the word ends in \textbf{-m} because the seeing reaches it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: -us and -er reach -um}
Three known nouns give you the useful masculine pattern:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{amīcus -> amīcum} — \textbf{amīcum adiuvō}, I help the friend
  \item \textbf{magister -> magistrum} — \textbf{magistrum audiō}, I hear the teacher
  \item \textbf{liber -> librum} — \textbf{librum legō}, I read the book
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Magister} and \textbf{liber} drop their nominative \textbf{-er} before \textbf{-um}. The genitives you learned — \emph{magistrī}, \emph{librī} — already showed the shorter stems \emph{magistr-} and \emph{libr-}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ending frees the order}]
\textbf{Librum legō} does not need English order to tell you what is read. The \textbf{-um} has already done that work.

Put the two lessons together: \textbf{epistulam scrībō; librum legō.} Two actions, two objects, two visible endings.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item amīcum adiuvō
  \item magistrum audiō
  \item librum legō
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the object form of \textbf{liber}? (\textbf{Librum.})

What ending do \textbf{amīcum}, \textbf{magistrum} and \textbf{librum} share? (\textbf{-um}, ending in the accusative \textbf{-m}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ad scholam; in scholā; domum]{ad scholam, in scholā, domum — toward, at, and homeward}

\label{lesson:LA-C59-place}



\begin{quote}
The form \textbf{scholam} is no longer new. Read it after a tiny word: \textbf{ad scholam}.

\textbf{Ad} points toward an endpoint: \textbf{ad scholam ambulō} — I walk to or toward school.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: motion and rest do not look alike}
These three short shapes carry a whole route:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{ad scholam ambulō} — I walk toward school
  \item \textbf{in scholā sedeō} — I sit in school
  \item \textbf{domum eō} — I go home
\end{itemize}

Motion \textbf{toward} takes \textbf{ad} plus the accusative \textbf{scholam}. Rest \textbf{in} a place takes \textbf{in} plus ablative \textbf{scholā}, whose long final \textbf{-ā} matters. \textbf{Domum} is the old compact exception: homeward needs no preposition.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: follow the case, then the journey}]
A reader can now follow three stages without translating every word: movement toward, rest inside, movement home.

Add the object from the last lesson: \textbf{in scholā librum legō}. The long \textbf{-ā} locates the action; \textbf{-um} shows what the reading reaches.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item ad scholam ambulō — movement toward
  \item in scholā sedeō — rest inside
  \item domum eō — movement home
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which form means \textquotedblleft{}in school\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{In scholā}, with long \textbf{-ā}.)

Which destination needs no preposition? (\textbf{Domum} — homeward.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(reading)]{(reading) — a whole meeting, one turn at a time}

\label{lesson:LA-C59-social-exchange}



\begin{quote}
The first passage was forty-two words. This exchange is seventy-three.

Do not race. Follow who asks, who answers, and where the two people go. The endings will keep the objects visible.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
\begin{quote}
— Salvē! — Salvē! — Quid tibi nōmen est? — Mihi nōmen est Iūlia. Quid tibi nōmen est? — Mihi nōmen est Mārcus. — Quōmodo valēs? — Bene valeō. Et tū? — Bene valeō. — Ubi schola tua est? — Schola mea ibi est. Ubi schola tua est? — Schola mea hic est. — Māne ad scholam ambulō. In scholā sedeō. — Ego māne librum legō. Post merīdiem epistulam scrībō. — Librum iterum legō. — Cūr? — Quia liber meus bonus est. — Bene. — Crās tē vidēbō. — Ita. Valē! — Valē!
\end{quote}

Read once for the route: names, wellbeing, school, work, reason, farewell.

Read again and find the two things handled: \textbf{librum} and \textbf{epistulam}.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a dialogue is a chain of answers}]
You do not need to translate every turn. \textbf{Quid tibi nōmen est?} predicts a name. \textbf{Quōmodo valēs?} predicts wellbeing. \textbf{Ubi} predicts a place. \textbf{Cūr?} predicts \textbf{quia}.

That prediction is reading. It lets the shape of one turn prepare you for the next.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the exchange once, preserving each turn
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does the first speaker's school stand? (\textbf{Ibi} — there.)

Why is the book read again? (\textbf{Quia liber meus bonus est.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(reading)]{(reading) — diēs meus, my day}

\label{lesson:LA-C59-dies-meus}



\begin{quote}
The exchange gave you seventy-three words in turns. This account gives you one hundred forty words in one voice.

First follow the day words. Then follow the objects. You already know every form.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
\begin{quote}
Nōmen meum est Mārcus. Ego sum discipulus. Domus mea bona est. Canis meus hic est, et fēlēs mea ibi est. Māne prīma hōra est. Ego stō, lac bibō, et mel et ōvum edō. Portam aperiō et portam claudō, et ad scholam ambulō. Schola mea bona est. In scholā sedeō. Magister meus bonus est. Magistrum videō et audiō. Prīmum librum accipiō et legō. Secundum librum nōn accipiō, quia secundus liber malus est. Epistulam scrībō. Cōgitō et intellegō. Amīcum meum videō et adiuvō. Amīcus meus discipulus est. Sexta hōra est. Lac bibō, et mel et ōvum edō. Vīnum nōn bibō. Aquam bibō. Mare et caelum videō. Post merīdiem domum eō. Hic sedeō, et librum iterum legō. Cūr iterum legō? Quia liber meus bonus est. Vesper est. Nox est. Bene valeō. Dormiō. Crās iterum ad scholam veniō. Crās magistrum et amīcum meum videō.
\end{quote}

Read once for time: morning, first hour, sixth hour, after midday, evening, night, tomorrow.

Read again for the route: home, toward school, in school, homeward.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the account has two maps}]
The time words make one map. The place phrases make another. Inside both, the object endings tell you what each action reaches: \textbf{portam}, \textbf{magistrum}, \textbf{librum}, \textbf{epistulam}, \textbf{amīcum}, \textbf{aquam}.

The account repeats \textbf{librum} for a reason. The first book is read; the second is refused; the good book is read again. That is a connected thread, not a list of unrelated sentences.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the account once, pausing only at full stops
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Put the route in order. (\textbf{Domus — ad scholam — in scholā — domum.})

What happens tomorrow? (\textbf{He goes to school again and sees his teacher and friend.})
\end{tcolorbox}
